{
  "hexsha": "0f71f852a96af9685858ce59fda34ecbf85c283d",
  "one_line_summary": "phonet: pep: fix use-after-free in pep_get_sb()",
  "vulnerability_summary": "pep_get_sb() calls pskb_may_pull() which may relocate skb head data, then dereferences the stale pointer ph obtained before the pull, causing a slab use-after-free read.",
  "vulnerability_pattern": "Code saves a pointer to skb header data, calls pskb_may_pull() which may reallocate and invalidate that pointer, then dereferences the stale pointer afterward.",
  "patch": "commit 0f71f852a96af9685858ce59fda34ecbf85c283d
Author: Breno Leitao <leitao@debian.org>
Date:   Tue Jul 21 01:58:45 2026 -0700

    phonet: pep: fix use-after-free in pep_get_sb()
    
    pep_get_sb() doesn't consider that pskb_may_pull() might have relocated
    the skb data, and continue to access the older pointer, causing UAF.
    
    Reproduced under KASAN:
    
      BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in pep_get_sb+0x234/0x3b0
      Read of size 1 at addr ff11000105510f50 by task repro/157
       pep_get_sb+0x234/0x3b0
       pipe_handler_do_rcv+0x5f7/0xa10
       pep_do_rcv+0x203/0x410
       __sk_receive_skb+0x471/0x4a0
       phonet_rcv+0x5b3/0x6c0
       __netif_receive_skb+0xcc/0x1d0
    
    Refetch the header with skb_header_pointer() after pskb_may_pull(), so
    the possibly stale pointer is no longer dereferenced. There are better
    ways to solve this, but, this is the less instrusive one.
    
    Fixes: 9641458d3ec4 ("Phonet: Pipe End Point for Phonet Pipes protocol")
    Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
    Signed-off-by: Breno Leitao <leitao@debian.org>
    Link: https://patch.msgid.link/20260721-phonet_get_sb_uaf-v1-1-95fd7881cc4e@debian.org
    Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>

diff --git a/net/phonet/pep.c b/net/phonet/pep.c
index 706927139393..31b29e3ca7bc 100644
--- a/net/phonet/pep.c
+++ b/net/phonet/pep.c
@@ -55,6 +55,8 @@ static unsigned char *pep_get_sb(struct sk_buff *skb, u8 *ptype, u8 *plen,
 	ph = skb_header_pointer(skb, 0, 2, &h);
 	if (ph == NULL || ph->sb_len < 2 || !pskb_may_pull(skb, ph->sb_len))
 		return NULL;
+	/* pskb_may_pull() may have reallocated the head; refetch ph. */
+	ph = skb_header_pointer(skb, 0, 2, &h);
 	ph->sb_len -= 2;
 	*ptype = ph->sb_type;
 	*plen = ph->sb_len;
"
}

These are byte reads of the linear head. The branch definition says dereference includes "any ->field read". So even single-field reads count per the branch definition ("any ->field read, struct-sized copy, memcmp/memcpy of 2 or more bytes, or of a variable-length header...").

Also note: the "validated-equals-used" invariant — ncsi_validate_rsp_pkt validates length vs payload but never ensures the skb actually contains that many linear bytes.

Now, is the skb non-linear at the ptype delivery point? A normal NCSI device (e.g. NC-SI pass-through NIC like ftgmac100, or mellanox) receives frames via NAPI; RX skbs are typically linear (single frag) for normal MTU frames. But GRO can coalesce; NCSI ethertype 0x88F8 wouldn't be GRO-merged by typical drivers. However, the branch says report sites "reachable by a remote attacker with a crafted non-linear (frag/fraglist/GRO/scatter-gather) skb". Non-linear RX skbs are possible via:
- Drivers that use page frags for RX (e.g. some with build_skb over pages... typically still linear for small frames).

- macvlan/bonding forwarding of a non-linear skb from another netdev — e.g., a packet injected via another ptype handler? Not typical.

The honest reachability question: In practice, an attacker "remote" for NCSI means on the NC-SI management network side. The NCSI packet_type is registered on the specific NCSI-capable netdev (ptype.dev = dev). The remote attacker is whoever can send Ethernet frames to that NIC's management channel. Whether the skb is non-linear depends on the RX driver. Many NIC drivers allocate linear skbs for small frames. But some drivers (e.g. those using page-based RX with frags, like certain 10G drivers) produce non-linear skbs when the frame spans multiple buffers — typically only for large frames (e.g., > ~1 page or with LRO). NCSI frames are small (max payload 512? Actually NCSI max packet ~ 1500ish). Hmm.
